UniCredit stock: Results and US bond issue shape weekly focus
sum: UniCredit's week was defined by strong third-quarter results and a return to the US funding market. On Monday, November 9, the bank reported record quarterly performance and lifted its fiscal 2026 net profit ambition. On Friday, November 13, it announced a USD 3.5 billion senior non-preferred issuance.

In its November 9 results release, UniCredit said third-quarter net profit increased 24 percent year on year to 3.3 billion euros. Revenue rose 12 percent to 6.9 billion euros, while return on tangible equity reached 25.5 percent.

The bank raised its fiscal 2026 net profit ambition to well above 11.5 billion euros before extraordinary charges. Nine-month net profit reached 9.4 billion euros, and organic capital generation stood at 8.2 billion euros. UniCredit also said remaining approvals for its Commerzbank plans were expected by late November, with new governance targeted for the first quarter of 2027 after settlement and control.

On November 13, UniCredit announced in its US fixed-income release that it had issued USD 3.5 billion of senior non-preferred notes. Demand exceeded USD 20 billion from more than 200 investors, according to the bank. The transaction is its first US issuance since 2021 and starts pre-funding for 2027 requirements.

The issue comprises three tranches with initial coupons of 5.970 percent, 6.201 percent and 6.585 percent. Settlement is expected on November 19, 2026. For investors, the transaction adds a funding milestone to a week already marked by higher earnings expectations and a larger interim distribution.
UniCredit stock traded at 83.78 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 12:36 CET on Saturday, November 14, 2026.
Broader market developments are covered in the Current market reports.

UniCredit stock returns to US market with USD 3.5 billion issue
sum: UniCredit is returning to the US fixed-income market with a multi-tranche senior non-preferred issuance totaling USD 3.5 billion, according to a company release published in Milan on Friday, November 13, 2026. The transaction is the Italian bank's first issuance in the US market since 2021 and starts pre-funding for its 2027 funding needs.

Demand exceeded USD 20 billion from more than 200 investors worldwide, the release said. North American investors accounted for about 65% of demand, allowing UniCredit to tighten initial price guidance before setting the final terms.

The offering consists of three fixed-to-fixed-rate notes. A USD 1.5 billion tranche with a four-year maturity and a three-year call carries an initial annual coupon of 5.970%. A USD 1 billion tranche with a six-year maturity and a five-year call carries a 6.201% coupon, while a further USD 1 billion tranche with an 11-year maturity and a 10-year call carries a 6.585% coupon.

The coupons are payable semi-annually. If UniCredit does not redeem the notes at the first call date, the coupons reset to the one-year US Treasury rate plus the applicable spread. Those spreads are 105 basis points for the shortest tranche, 125 basis points for the middle tranche and 148 basis points for the longest tranche. Each tranche was issued and re-offered at 100.00%.

The notes will be issued under UniCredit's GMTN Programme and are eligible for MREL purposes, helping reinforce the bank's funding structure across maturities. The expected ratings are Baa2 from Moody's, BBB from S&P and BBB+ from Fitch. The minimum denomination is USD 250,000, with further increments of USD 1,000.

Only qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A and investors outside the United States under Regulation S or another exemption may buy the notes. Settlement is expected on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Citigroup, J.P. Morgan and UniCredit acted as global coordinators, with seven other banks serving as joint bookrunners.
UniCredit stock traded at 84.25 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:04 CET on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Commerzbank stock: UniCredit clearance decision nears
sum: UniCredit's path to control of Commerzbank is entering a decisive regulatory phase. Reuters reported on Monday, November 9, that the Italian bank is set to secure unconditional EU antitrust approval for its acquisition of Germany's second-largest lender, citing three people with direct knowledge of the matter. The European Commission and UniCredit declined to comment.

Commerzbank stock traded at 39.80 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 10:49 CET on Thursday, November 12, 2026, 0.90 percent below the Xetra close of Wednesday, November 11. The quote reflects the market's current positioning while investors await the next regulatory milestones; it does not by itself establish a causal reaction to the takeover process.

The European Commission, the EU competition authority, is due to decide on the transaction by November 16. Its approval would follow the European Central Bank's green light last month and remove a major regulatory obstacle to UniCredit's plan to take control of Commerzbank.

UniCredit chief executive Andrea Orcel said on November 9 that all remaining regulatory approvals would arrive before the end of November, sooner than previously anticipated. The timetable keeps the takeover in focus for Commerzbank shareholders because the next approvals would determine when UniCredit can move from a large strategic holding toward effective control.

A separate legal issue concerns Berlin's demand to retain two seats on Commerzbank's supervisory board. Reuters reported that UniCredit has challenged the demand and wants to appoint all 10 shareholder representatives on the 20-member board. The dispute is separate from the Commission's merger assessment but could influence the structure of future cross-border transactions.

The German government has reduced its holding, acquired during the 2009 rescue, to 13.3 percent. Its focus has shifted toward safeguards for jobs, lending to small and medium-sized companies, Commerzbank's Frankfurt headquarters and the bank's stock-market listing.
For investors, the November timetable links regulatory progress with a possible change in Commerzbank's governance.

UniCredit stock: Profit rises 24% as Commerzbank control nears
sum: UniCredit reported its strongest quarter on record on Monday, November 9, 2026, as net profit rose 24 percent year on year to 3.3 billion euros. The Italian bank also raised its full-year profit ambition and set out the next steps toward control of Germany's Commerzbank.

The results were published by UniCredit. Third-quarter revenue increased 12 percent to 6.9 billion euros, with core revenue accounting for 90 percent of the total. Costs fell 1 percent despite continued investment, producing a 32.8 percent cost-income ratio.

Net profit for the first nine months reached 9.4 billion euros, up 7 percent year on year, or 16 percent after adjusting for a positive one-off recorded in the second quarter of 2025. Return on tangible equity stood at 25.5 percent in the third quarter and 24.3 percent for the nine-month period.

UniCredit raised its 2026 net profit ambition to well above 11.5 billion euros before extraordinary charges. The bank maintained its standalone ambitions of net profit above 13 billion euros in 2028 and above 15 billion euros in 2030, with return on tangible equity around 25 percent in those longer-term targets.

Chief Executive Andrea Orcel said the performance reflected growth, cost efficiency, disciplined capital allocation and a strong balance sheet. The bank said loans grew 9 percent and deposits 7 percent at the end of the quarter, while its nine-month cost of risk remained within its target range at 17 basis points.

UniCredit expects the remaining regulatory approvals for its Commerzbank plans by late November. After settlement, it intends to request an extraordinary general meeting to elect new supervisory board members. New governance and the launch of the Commerzbank Unlocked programme are expected in the first quarter of 2027, subject to approvals and the meeting timetable.

The bank said its 2026 distribution would remain unaffected by the transaction. Assuming settlement and a Commerzbank stake of around 50 percent, UniCredit expects earnings per share above 10 euros and distributions per share above 8 euros in 2028. Those figures are illustrative rather than a profit forecast, and a possible combination with HypoVereinsbank remains subject to corporate and regulatory approvals.

Commerzbank Buyback Rolls On as UniCredit's Boardroom Math Takes Shape
sum: Commerzbank repurchased 2,882,652 of its own shares during the buyback week running through Friday, keeping capital returns flowing to shareholders even as its largest suitor plots a sweeping overhaul of how the bank is run.

The purchases, disclosed in a capital markets notice, came on every trading day of the past week. They land against a backdrop of mounting anticipation over UniCredit's next move: the Italian lender expects the remaining takeover approvals to arrive by the end of November.

Once the offer settles, UniCredit's stake is set to climb from just under 30% to just under 50%. Chief executive Andrea Orcel intends to stay just below 50% plus one share, meaning the influence he is buying will be exercised chiefly through the company's governing bodies rather than through outright ownership.

That makes the supervisory board the real battleground. UniCredit wants to appoint all ten shareholder representatives, while Berlin — which holds 13.3% of Commerzbank — is claiming two seats. Reuters reported that EU reviewers initially raised legal concerns about Germany's right to nominate directors.

Orcel plans to convene an extraordinary general meeting in the first quarter of 2027 to elect new supervisory board members, with the new leadership structure and the "Commerzbank Unlocked" programme launching in the same window. According to his account, such a meeting is normally held 30 to 40 days after it is convened — another organisational step between regulatory clearance and a reconstituted board.

The stock took heart from the detail. Commerzbank shares rose 5.1% to close at €39.95, with Reuters attributing the gain to UniCredit's quarterly figures and its comments on expanding its supervisory board influence.

Those figures were formidable: UniCredit reported a net profit of €3.3 billion for the third quarter of 2026. Morningstar, however, flagged the substantial contribution from trading gains, dividend income and a low tax rate — a reminder that earnings quality matters as much as the headline number when judging whether the takeover plan can be financed and sustained.

sum: Commerzbank shareholders have two fresh data points to weigh against each other this week: a modest regulatory break from Frankfurt and a pair of trimmed price targets from London and Toronto. The first offers breathing room on capital. The second reflects a harder truth about what the bank can earn on deposits.

The European Central Bank confirmed on 27 October that it will lower the lender's additional Pillar 2 own-funds requirement by 5 basis points to 2.10% for 2027. The relief is real but small. It matters most if earnings hold up well enough to keep funding both the capital base and the share buyback now in progress.

DZ Bank cut Commerzbank from "Buy" to "Hold" on Thursday, with media reports putting the new fair value at EUR 40, down from EUR 46. Analyst Philipp Häßler pointed to the bank's comments on net interest income and the absence of near-term share-price catalysts. The looming UniCredit question, he added, remains the dominant theme.

RBC Capital Markets moved in the same direction the same day, lowering its target to EUR 39 from EUR 41 while keeping a "Sector Perform" rating. Analyst Anke Reingen flagged uncertainty over the short-term consequences of a possible UniCredit takeover, alongside waning confidence in the net interest income outlook.

Both downgrades landed hours after Commerzbank revised its net interest income forecast, citing competition for customer deposits. The bank now expects around EUR 8.5 billion for 2026, down from roughly EUR 8.6 billion previously.

That revision sits alongside an otherwise strong set of numbers. Third-quarter 2026 net profit rose to EUR 859 million, an increase of about 45% year on year, while operating profit for the quarter reached EUR 1.31 billion, up 25%. Reuters reported that the quarterly figures came in slightly below analyst expectations. Even so, the bank posted the best nine-month result in its history.

Over the first nine months of 2026, operating profit climbed 17% to EUR 4,037 million and net profit reached EUR 2.7 billion, 41% higher. Management reaffirmed its full-year target of at least EUR 3.4 billion in net profit.

sum: Cariverona is assessing how it could contribute to UniCredit's next governance structure, adding shareholder scrutiny to a leadership transition that will culminate with the bank's board renewal in spring 2027. The foundation's chairman, Bruno Giordano, made the comments on October 30 on the sidelines of Italy's Savings Day, according to Il Sole 24 Ore.

Giordano said Cariverona would make its assessment independently, guided by the quality of governance, the stability of the bank and long-term value creation. He did not rule out any option available under the regulatory and statutory framework, including a possible role in preparing candidate lists.

Cariverona has been a long-standing UniCredit shareholder and holds a stake of approximately 0.7 percent, according to the report. The foundation has maintained the position of a financial investor while monitoring developments at the bank. Its comments therefore leave open whether it will seek a more active role in shaping the next board.

Chairman Pier Carlo Padoan is due to leave at the end of his term for personal reasons. UniCredit's senior management is scheduled for renewal in spring 2027, and the bank will also have to choose a new chairman. No successor was named in the report.

The succession process puts governance continuity at the center of the investor debate. Cariverona's emphasis on independence and soundness points to the criteria it will apply as the next board structure takes shape, while the final outcome will depend on the nomination process and the subsequent shareholder vote.

sum: Commerzbank's capital story and its strategic story are running on separate tracks, and investors heading into the bank's third-quarter report will have to weigh both. On one side sits a share buyback that is actually being executed and a modest regulatory reprieve from the ECB. On the other sits the question that Handelsblatt reported yesterday is keeping investors on the sidelines: what UniCredit's planned takeover means for the bank's future direction.

Start with the capital side, because it is the part backed by hard numbers. In the reporting window from October 26 through October 30 inclusive, Commerzbank bought back 3,316,027 of its own shares. Cumulative purchases under the running programme reached 21,268,730 shares by the end of that period, a figure that measures progress to date rather than a total volume or its full exhaustion. The programme itself dates back to September 4.

Those disclosures document capital deployment — nothing more. A buyback report is not an earnings release, and no one should read a higher profit or an improved business trajectory into the pace of repurchases.

The ECB decision, announced about a week ago, operates on a different plane entirely. It concerns supervisory capital: the Pillar 2 additional own-funds requirement will fall by 5 basis points to 2.10% of total capital for 2027. The new SREP decision applies from January 1, 2027, and the minimum hard-core capital requirement for the maximum distributable amount comes to a pro forma 10.26% of risk-weighted assets, based on the position as of June 30, 2026.

Relief of this kind is regulatory in nature. It is not a profit forecast, and it would be a stretch to infer extra distributions from it — a lower minimum threshold and an actual decision on how to deploy capital are distinct matters. What the easing can do is support the assessment of the capital position; it cannot stand in for a convincing operating outlook.

That distinction matters because of the overhang described by Handelsblatt. Investor reticence, the paper reported, stems chiefly from the planned UniCredit takeover and uncertainty over where Commerzbank is headed.

sum: Commerzbank bought back 3,157,027 of its own shares, the bank reported on Monday, with the purchases running from 12 through 16 October under its ongoing repurchase programme. The disclosure lands alongside a separate signal that may matter more to the equity story: German corporate treasurers are growing warier of UniCredit's takeover plans, and at least one rival is already circling their business.

The shares fell 4.3% yesterday as a Europe-wide selloff swept through bank stocks. Reuters put the decline in the Eurozone banks index at 4.2%, its weakest session since March. That context matters for how the move should be read — the drop reflects sector pressure rather than any fresh operating announcement from Commerzbank itself. A broad retreat across bank equities explains the immediate trading, but it says nothing about whether the lender can set an independent counterweight through its own business performance.

Against that weak backdrop stands a capital measure that has actually been carried out rather than merely announced. Even so, the buyback offers no assurance on the share price: yesterday's action shows the programme did not shield the stock from the latest selling. Nor does the acquisition of own shares say anything about forthcoming results. Should those fall short of investor expectations, the repurchase may not offset a more critical assessment, and a mere calming of the sector would not by itself mark a durable turning point.

The next concrete checkpoint is the release of third-quarter 2026 results on 5 November 2026. What counts is whether business development provides a solid basis for valuation. A recovery in the banking sector could help, but a company-specific re-rating would also require convincing figures. Investors should keep those two possible impulses apart rather than reading any rebound as automatic confirmation of operating strength. In the favourable case, strong quarterly numbers and easing selling pressure in the sector would coincide, with the running buyback acting as an additional positive factor — a combination more meaningful than a rally carried solely by the wider market.
The takeover debate adds a business risk to the regulatory questions.

items.t: UniCredit plans EUR 1.00 billion bond redemption: UniCredit stock falls 3.05 percent
sum: UniCredit plans to redeem EUR 1.00 billion of green notes early on November 15, 2026, while its stock was trading at EUR 72.88 at Lang & Schwarz on October 22, 2026, 3.05 percent below the Xetra close of October 21, 2026. MarketScreener reported that UniCredit intends to redeem its fixed-to-floating-rate green callable non-preferred senior notes, subject to authorization from the Single Resolution Board.

The notes were issued on November 15, 2022 and were due to mature on November 15, 2027. UniCredit plans to redeem them at par with accrued and unpaid interest, after which interest will stop accruing, according to MarketScreener.

The latest reported operating picture remains profitable. In the second quarter of 2026, revenue was EUR 6.456 billion and net income was EUR 2.954 billion, compared with EUR 6.934 billion of revenue and EUR 3.264 billion of net income in the first quarter of 2026, based on the financial information on UniCredit. The quarter-on-quarter comparison shows lower revenue and net income, giving the November results a clear test beyond the bond action.

UniCredit's recent chronology runs from the October 9, 2026 decision to move third-quarter board approval to November 8, through the October 16, 2026 approval covering a stake above 30.00 percent in Commerzbank, to the October 20, 2026 announcement of the EUR 1.00 billion bond redemption. The approval was reported by MarketScreener, while the bond terms came from Alliance News through the linked report.

UniCredit said on October 9, 2026 that the board will approve third-quarter results on November 8, 2026. The group results presentation and conference call follow on November 9, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. CET. The timing matters because the second-quarter net profit of EUR 2.954 billion sets a concrete profitability benchmark for the next report.

sum: Commerzbank's buyback machine keeps running on its own track, and that is precisely the point. The Frankfurt lender disclosed on Monday that it has repurchased 14,271,110 of its own shares since September 4, a figure that reflects completed transactions rather than any fresh decision to return capital. Just 3,157,027 of those shares changed hands in the past week alone.

The mandatory disclosure matters for what it does not say. It carries no additional commitment to future purchases, and it offers no read on how UniCredit's long-running pursuit will end. Investors who treat buyback volume as a proxy for takeover momentum are reading the wrong document.

UniCredit's own disclosure arrived roughly a week earlier: the European Central Bank has cleared the Italian bank to push past the 30 percent threshold in Commerzbank, with no cap on how far it may go. That permission opens room to act. It does not confirm that every regulatory process has closed, and it certainly does not mean the stake has already been assembled.

What UniCredit has is an expectation. It anticipates the remaining approvals and conditions for its offer to be settled by year-end, at which point it reckons on holding around 50 percent of the voting rights — enough to take control. That number is a projection, not a position on the register. The gap between an ECB green light and an achieved controlling stake is where the entire investment case currently sits.

Political noise has been folded into the same open process. German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, according to media reports on Friday, described the talks as constructive, touching on Frankfurt as a location, the interests of employees, and financing for small and medium-sized businesses. A favourable account of a conversation is not a signed agreement, and it should not be filed as one.

For shareholders, the test is whether fresh news advances completion in concrete terms or merely restates a known intention. A confirmed step forward carries different information value than a repeated affirmation of the target — and conflating the two risks pricing the same progress twice. The year-end timeline, too, remains the company's own expectation; no fixed completion date has been established, and no control transfer has occurred.

sum: The rise in yields over the last few trading sessions is unsettling the markets. Meanwhile, tensions in the Middle East are keeping energy prices high: gas prices rose by 6.4 per cent over the week, whilst Brent crude rose by 2 per cent

(Il Sole 24 Ore Radiocor) - A turbulent week for European stock markets, which ended the week in the red, weighed down by the rise in government bond yields that is spooking the markets. Investors must also contend with energy commodity prices that continue to rise (Brent up 2% over the week, WTI up 0.9% and gas in Amsterdam up 6.4%), with inflation exceeding expectations and the geopolitical crisis in the Middle East. These factors risk leading – if not immediately, then at least in the longer term – to central banks raising interest rates more rapidly than anticipated. Consequently, the FTSE MIB in Milan was the worst performer in Europe, down 4.1 per cent for the week, dragged down by the performance of banking shares, followed by the CAC in Paris – under pressure from political and budgetary uncertainties in France – and by Madrid’s IBEX (both down 3.4 per cent). The Frankfurt DAX (-1.2 per cent) and the London FTSE 100 (-1.3 per cent) also recorded losses.

At sector level, in Europe sales are hitting the banking sector (-7%), which is grappling with the challenge of government bond yields: as they hold large quantities of government bonds, the rise in interest rates is effectively devaluing their portfolios. Furthermore, an increase in sovereign risk also tends to raise the cost of funding and the perceived credit risk. Conversely, buying is driving up tech shares (+4.3%) and oil & gas shares (+3%).

Turning our attention to the Milan Stock Exchange, it is the banking shares that have recorded the worst performances in a week marked by new developments on the ‘Risiko’ front. In particular, Delfin, Caltagirone and Benetton have rejected the two-pronged move by MPS CEO Luigi Lovaglio regarding Banco BPM and Banca Generali, designed to defend Siena from the hostile takeover bid launched by Intesa Sanpaolo. Consequently, Mediobanca fell by 13.1 per cent during the week, Banco BPM by 10.2 per cent, Intesa by 9.9 per cent and UniCredit by 9.3 per cent.

sum: The next hard number on Commerzbank's calendar arrives on 5 November 2026, when the Frankfurt lender publishes its third-quarter results. After months in which speculation about a possible move by Italy's UniCredit dominated the conversation, that date shifts attention back to the unglamorous question of whether the bank can keep earning at its current pace.

Analysts, for their part, have been trimming their enthusiasm. Deutsche Bank Research cut the stock to "Hold" from "Buy" on 30 September, with analyst Benjamin Goy keeping his price target at EUR 42 but arguing that the remaining upside is limited. In his view, the key drivers that carried the shares higher — rising net interest income and shareholder payouts — are now largely priced in or already delivered.

RBC Capital Markets followed on 2 October, downgrading the stock to "Sector Perform" from "Outperform" and lowering its target to EUR 40 from EUR 43. The brokerage pointed to higher execution risk stemming from UniCredit's intentions, alongside increased cost of equity and operational uncertainties tied to the ambitions of the major shareholder.

The political backdrop has grown more explicit. Roughly a week before the RBC move, the German government asked UniCredit for firm commitments in the event of an agreed takeover. According to Reuters, Berlin wants the bank to remain listed, to keep its base in Frankfurt and to expand its lending to small and medium-sized enterprises, with major decisions continuing to be made on German soil. UniCredit welcomed the dialogue but made clear that talks are not yet concluded.

That standoff explains part of the market's caution. UniCredit's plans had at times pushed the share price higher, but the operational and strategic hurdles are now drawing more scrutiny than the deal chatter itself.

Trading has reflected the cooler mood. The stock closed at EUR 39.86 on the most recent Tuesday, a gain of 1.5% on the previous session, leaving it 8.0% below its 52-week high of EUR 43.34. In a separate reading, the shares were quoted at EUR 39.34, down 1.3% on the day.
Management, meanwhile, is trying to make its own case. Chief executive Bettina Orlopp reaffirmed the group's standalone strategy in an interview and stressed its commitment to the Swiss business.

items.t: Putin clears UniCredit’s Russian bank restructuring and sale to UAE investor
sum: Russian President Vladimir Putin has approved UniCredit Group’s plan to reorganize its Russian banking business and carry out transactions that could lead to the sale of part of the Italian lender’s operations to a private investor from the United Arab Emirates.

The order, signed Oct. 5 and published on Russia’s official legal information portal, allows UniCredit Bank Russia to be split into separate entities and permits the transfer of UniCredit’s 100% stake in the remaining business.

UniCredit announced in May that it planned to separate part of its Russian operations into a new entity, known as the "New Bank," while the remaining activities would stay in another entity, the "Remaining Bank."

Under the proposed structure, UniCredit would retain 100% ownership of the New Bank, while a buyer would take full ownership of the Remaining Bank. The transaction is planned for the first half of 2027, subject to a binding agreement, the separation of Russian assets and regulatory approvals.

Putin’s latest order specifically authorizes the restructuring and the acquisition of shares by UniCredit’s sole shareholder, along with transactions involving the 100% stake held by UniCredit. The decree also states that no additional permits, approvals or consents required under Russian law will be needed to complete those transactions.

The move gives UniCredit an exemption from restrictions that have made it difficult for banks from countries Moscow considers "unfriendly" to sell Russian assets. Foreign shareholders generally face restrictions on transactions involving shares in Russian banks, although the Russian president can approve individual sales.

UniCredit described the prospective buyer in May as an established private investor in the UAE with long-standing connections to the local business community. The Italian group also indicated that it had carried out the required compliance checks.

For UniCredit shareholders, the potential Banco BPM operation introduces both opportunity and risk: a successful deal could expand UniCredit’s franchise and fee income base, while any prolonged negotiations or regulatory hurdles might weigh on capital planning and temporarily increase volatility in UniCredit stock.

As Ad-hoc News reported, UniCredit held an extraordinary shareholders meeting in Milan on September 21, 2026, with voting organized via a designated proxy holder, following a session on September 18, 2026 when the stock closed at EUR 81.13 on the Milan Stock Exchange, down 3.05 percent from the prior day.

Commerzbank's Dublin Signal: Brussels Pushes Cross-Border Deals as Orlopp Bets on 2027 Margins
sum: European finance ministers and central bank governors gathered in Dublin on Friday to chew over a European Commission report that urges the continent's lenders to bulk up — a discussion that lands squarely on Commerzbank, where UniCredit's long-running courtship has been stalled by Berlin since June.

ECB Vice President Boris Vujcic used the Dublin platform to argue that euro-area banks need deeper capital markets and greater scale to compete with their US peers. Greece's representative Pierrakakis supplied the hard number behind that case: America's largest banks plough more than 2.5 times as much into information technology relative to their assets as EU institutions do. The Commission's paper accordingly calls for curbing political interference in bank mergers and dismantling barriers to cross-border business.

That recommendation reads like a direct reference to the German-Italian standoff. Berlin rejected UniCredit's approach in June, a campaign the Milan-based group has pursued since September 2024. Vujcic stopped short of endorsing lighter capital requirements as a trade-off for size, but the broader pressure to stop national governments from blocking deals points straight at the Commerzbank file.

Momentum on the Italian side shows no sign of fading. UniCredit chief Andrea Orcel met German Finance Minister Klingbeil on Monday to discuss the Commerzbank dossier — a sit-down after which the target's shares shed roughly 5.0%. On Friday, Italy's economy minister Giorgetti also took up the Commerzbank question with Orcel, according to reports from Milan.

UniCredit's stated ambitions are considerable: once the ECB gives the green light, the group expects to hold somewhere between just over 30% and nearly 50% of Commerzbank. It has already secured access to as much as 49.65% of the shares.

Commerzbank CEO Bettina Orlopp, for her part, has signalled openness to cooperation around targets for 2028 and 2030, while insisting on running the bank independently through 2028. Any integration with HypoVereinsbank would not begin before 2029 under UniCredit's planning. The German state retains roughly 13.3% of Commerzbank — other figures put the holding at around 12% to 13% — and is demanding two supervisory board seats.

items.t: Allianz Holds Near Record High as Buybacks, Waymo Deal and a Busy Conference Calendar Converge
sum: Allianz shares continue to trade at elevated levels, closing Wednesday at EUR 449.90 after a 1.2% gain — a print that leaves the stock just 1.0% shy of its 52-week peak of EUR 454.50. The steadiness comes despite a noticeably more cautious tone from parts of the analyst community, a tension that market participants appear content to weigh against the underlying resilience of the business.

One persistent support for the share price has been the insurer's own appetite for its stock. Between 31 August and 4 September inclusive, the company repurchased 190,580 of its own shares on Xetra and selected European venues. The purchases form part of an ongoing buyback programme that is proceeding to plan, steadily withdrawing paper from free float and tightening available supply. For shareholders, the message is a familiar one: capital is being returned directly to owners, even as external growth initiatives take on greater prominence.

On the strategic front, Allianz Partners and Waymo unveiled a collaboration covering insurance for autonomous vehicles alongside joint safety research in Europe — a push into a mobility segment that sits well outside the group's traditional underwriting base. The move is not isolated. Roughly two weeks ago the group submitted an offer for AA, while more than a month has passed since the ECB granted UniCredit permission for the Danish Compromise, a decision that has since translated into a gain of 27.7% for UniCredit.

Risk management in the core business remains under the microscope. According to a Reuters report, Zurich Insurance Group and Allianz provided cover on transactions involving the distressed iron ore trader Radiant World. The news agency reported on 11 September that subsidiary Allianz Trade additionally insured the trading firm against payment defaults.

Analyst sentiment has hardly turned uniformly bullish. Barclays raised its price target modestly, as reported by Reuters on 4 September, yet a number of market observers continue to counsel restraint. The more downbeat stance out of the research community has done little to derail the stock's trajectory on European trading floors, with investors apparently balancing the cooler assessments against the stability of the franchise.

sum: Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.
The German government formally rejected UniCredit's unsolicited €24 billion (about $28 billion) all-stock buyout offer for Commerzbank AG as the initial tender window closed on Tuesday, June 16.
Citing a lack of an appropriate premium and condemning what it termed an aggressive approach by the Italian lender, Berlin robustly endorsed Commerzbank's strategy for corporate independence.

The high-stakes takeover battle has escalated into a legal dispute, with Frankfurt prosecutors launching a preliminary market manipulation investigation into UniCredit's complex use of derivative hedges to accumulate its massive position.

The interministerial steering committee managing Germany's state stabilization fund delivered its decisive veto just hours before the midnight Frankfurt deadline. The German government, which remains Commerzbank's second-largest shareholder with an approximate 13% crisis-era rescue stake, declared that accepting the offer was non-viable from a financial standpoint.

The state finance agency emphasized Commerzbank's critical macroeconomic role as a primary capital provider for Germany's medium-sized Mittelstand corporate sector and its structural importance as a major employer in the Frankfurt financial hub.

Despite Berlin's fierce public opposition, UniCredit announced that valid acceptances under the voluntary buyout offer stood at 12.41% at the standard mid-day cut-off. When combined with its previously built 26.77% direct equity stake and 3.22% in share-settled derivatives, the Italian bank has successfully secured control over 42.4% of Commerzbank's total capital.

items.t: Andrea Orcel: The banker in Europe who wants to do it all
sum: There’s a banker who’s taking the world by storm, dreaming of pan-European giants, throwing down the gauntlet to governments, and wanting to defy the unspoken rule that hostile takeovers are doomed from the start. His name is Andrea Orcel, he is the CEO of the Italian bank UniCredit, and on March 16 — with economic uncertainty running high due to the escalating Iran war — he launched an unsolicited €35 billion ($40 billion) takeover bid for Germany’s Commerzbank, a target he has had squarely in his sights for at least a year and a half.

That is, precisely, the same amount of time Berlin has been baring its teeth at the Italian executive, without managing to deter him: “Our message to Commerzbank today is it is now time to talk,” he told market analysts after announcing the takeover bid.

The UniCredit–Commerzbank episode encapsulates the European Union’s major dilemmas: the financial architecture needed to achieve political integration; the lingering national sovereignty concerns among member states, the mutualization of risks, and the debate over the creation of European megabanks that are too big to fail, recalling the trauma of the Great Recession. It is, inevitably, also a story of ambition.

“We have a European Union that must move towards political union,” explains Juan María Nin, an experienced banker, who was the former CEO of Spain’s CaixaBank and Sabadell and former director of Santander. “For that, economic union is necessary, and this is not possible without a banking union. We still don’t have a common Deposit Guarantee Fund, nor a single, financially endowed resolution mechanism to make it possible.”
In his view, and in line with the conclusions of the Draghi report, “if Europe wants to compete in the capital markets, it needs large banks like those in the United States.”

Europe suffers from over‑diagnosis and under‑treatment: theory calls for more integration and greater scale to compete in the global economy — a single market that truly applies to banking as well — but practice keeps colliding with reality.

It is one thing to launch a takeover, and quite another to be the target of one. UniCredit appeared unannounced on Commerzbank’s shareholder register in September 2024, acquiring a stake that eventually rose to 26% (28–29% including derivatives).

items.t: Commerzbank Shares Press Toward Record as CEO Signals End of UniCredit Resistance
sum: The long-running standoff between Commerzbank and UniCredit is entering what looks like its final chapter. Bettina Orlopp, who has spent months digging in against Andrea Orcel's advances, has now indicated she is prepared to talk — a shift that sent Frankfurt-listed shares to €38.98 on Tuesday, leaving the stock within striking distance of its 52-week peak of €39.22.

Investors are reading the change in tone as a clear signal: a negotiated outcome is drawing closer. Orlopp has laid out her terms, demanding a double-digit premium for shareholders and contractual guarantees protecting the bank's international network. Without those concessions, her willingness to engage is unlikely to translate into a deal.

All roads now lead to Thursday, when two events collide. Commerzbank publishes its second-quarter results, and shortly afterward Orlopp and Orcel are scheduled to hold their first formal meeting. The convergence of the earnings release and the boardroom summit means one date will carry the weight of both the bank's operational credibility and the future of its ownership.

The market has already begun pricing in a constructive outcome. Monday's session saw the stock close at €38.50, up 2.34 percent, and the momentum has carried through. With the record high of €39.18 — set in mid-July — now just a fraction away, traders are watching whether a strong earnings beat and a productive dialogue can push the shares through that ceiling and toward the €40 mark.

Any offer that undervalues the bank faces a formidable obstacle in Berlin. The German government holds roughly 12 percent of Commerzbank — the secondary article puts the figure at 12.72 percent — and is reportedly weighing an increase to 25 percent. Such a blocking minority would effectively scupper UniCredit's ability to execute a squeeze-out, which requires a 90 percent majority.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he will not use political means to block a merger, yet UniCredit still needs the cooperation of both management and minority shareholders. That dynamic, analysts suggest, is putting upward pressure on the price per share.

items.t: Commerzbank's Autumn Pivot: Record Earnings Meet a Softened Stance on UniCredit
sum: The mood inside Commerzbank's Frankfurt headquarters has shifted decisively. After months of resistance to UniCredit's advances, the German lender has effectively conceded that the Italian giant's pursuit will succeed — a change of heart that has pushed the share price to within striking distance of its 52-week high.

Vice chairman Michael Kotzbauer acknowledged in the bank's internal newsroom that the takeover battle has been lost, though he maintained the bank had fought well. The about-face follows an extended period of defiance, during which the board initially dismissed UniCredit's approach as undervaluing the franchise. Chief executive Bettina Orlopp has now signalled internally that she is open to engagement with Milan, a marked departure from earlier positioning.

The mechanics of the deal are falling into place. UniCredit already controls just under 48 percent of voting rights, supplemented by a further 11 percent held through financial instruments. The German state retains a stake of roughly 13 percent — the primary article puts the figure at 12.7 percent — meaning UniCredit could mathematically push past the 60 percent threshold should Berlin eventually sell down its remaining holding.

The European Central Bank appears to be leaning toward approval, according to an internal document already submitted to its Supervisory Board. Germany's BaFin classified UniCredit's application for a majority stake as complete at the end of July and forwarded it to Frankfurt's banking supervisor. Market observers anticipate an ECB decision this autumn, with additional clearances still required from EU competition authorities and the US Federal Reserve. Notably, 17.6 percent of Commerzbank shares had already been tendered by the early July deadline.

Orlopp, whose contract runs through 2029, confirmed ongoing discussions with UniCredit at Tuesday's banking summit in Frankfurt, describing a constructive strategy focused on value maximisation while cautioning against mishandling the situation.
The bid battle has overshadowed what is otherwise a stellar operational performance. First-half revenue rose 7 percent to EUR 6.5 billion, while net profit jumped 40 percent to EUR 1.8 billion.

EBRD and UniCredit Bulbank support FitSpo’s green expansion in Bulgaria
sum: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is supporting the expansion of FitSpo Nutrition OOD, a Bulgarian producer of functional food products, through an unfunded risk‑sharing agreement with UniCredit Bulbank.

Under the transaction, UniCredit Bulbank is providing €5.3 million in long‑term financing to FitSpo. The EBRD is participating by sharing risk on up to €2.7 million of the financing through its Risk Sharing Facility, helping to improve access to longer‑term funding for a growing local company.

UniCredit Bulbank has been a financial partner of FitSpo since the early stages of the company’s development and has supported the brand’s growth since its market launch. Through tailored financing structures and a swift execution process, the bank has played a key role in enabling the company to scale its operations and strengthen its market position in Bulgaria and abroad.

The financing will support FitSpo’s investment programme to expand and modernise its production facilities in Bulgaria. The project includes the procurement and installation of a new, fully automated production line, a high‑efficiency packaging line and associated equipment, as well as investments in a new innovative green production facility. Once completed, the investment is expected to double FitSpo’s annual production capacity, enabling it to meet rising demand in both domestic and export markets.

“Supporting the growth of innovative Bulgarian companies like FitSpo is part of the bank’s long-term commitment to the development of the local economy,” commented Borislav Bangeev, Director Corporates, UniCredit Bulbank. “We have been proud to stand behind the company since its early development, and this new financing demonstrates how strong banking partnerships can help businesses scale faster, invest in innovation and expand internationally.”

The investments financed by UniCredit Bulbank are fully aligned with the bank’s ESG strategy, supporting projects that promote energy efficiency, sustainable production and the transition to a low-carbon economy. By backing companies that invest in innovative and environmentally responsible technologies, the bank contributes to strengthening the competitiveness of the Bulgarian economy while supporting sustainable growth.

Commerzbank's Diplomatic Pivot: Record Profits Meet a Softer Berlin Line on UniCredit
sum: The political resistance to UniCredit's advance on Commerzbank is crumbling, and the timing could hardly be better for Frankfurt's second-largest lender. Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil has invited UniCredit chief Andrea Orcel to the federal finance ministry on 14 September — a striking reversal from July, when Berlin branded the Italian bank's approach "aggressive and hostile." The market took note, with Commerzbank shares climbing 2.2 percent to €40.56 on Wednesday.

The change in tone has been remarkably swift. Over the summer, government officials refused any engagement with UniCredit; now, according to Bloomberg, senior figures are open to discussing the sale of the remaining 12.7 percent state stake to the Italians — provided agreement is first reached on strategy and the future direction of the bank. A regulatory decision on the takeover approval is expected between September and October.

The thaw extends to Commerzbank's own leadership. Supervisory board chairman Jens Weidmann acknowledged in late July that the balance of power was clear and signalled a constructive dialogue with UniCredit. Formal talks between Orcel and Commerzbank CEO Bettina Orlopp followed in August, with Orlopp stating plainly: "We are ready for constructive talks with UniCredit." UniCredit has already secured 47.6 percent of Commerzbank's shares, according to its own disclosures from July.

The rapprochement arrives on the back of formidable financial results. Commerzbank nearly doubled its second-quarter net profit to €898 million, up from €462 million in the same period last year, putting the bank firmly on track to hit its full-year target of at least €3.4 billion. Management also unveiled plans for up to €1.2 billion in additional share buybacks — a demonstration that capital strength does not depend on the outcome of the takeover question.

That combination of record earnings and shareholder returns gives Commerzbank's management genuine leverage heading into discussions with UniCredit. Negotiating from a position of strength allows the bank to set conditions rather than merely react to them.
Not every voice at Commerzbank sounds conciliatory.

Unicredit, profit 2025 at 10.6 billion (+14%). 30 billion to shareholders in 3 years
sum: Unicredit files a record 2025 with a net profit of EUR 10.6 billion (+14%), above estimates. And, adjusting its own estimates upwards, it now promises shareholders EUR 30 billion in the next three years and EUR 50 billion in the next five.

The relevant figure is 2025 closes with results above market expectations, despite the fact that the bank booked non-recurring charges of EUR 1.4bn in the fourth quarter to support future profitability prospects. Fourth-quarter net profit thus closes at EUR 10.6bn, up 13.6% from 2024, and book profit at EUR 10.9bn (+12.3%), numbers that compare with targets set at EUR 10.5bn and EUR 10.7bn respectively.

On the revenue side, the picture remains solid but less expansive: total revenue stood at EUR 24.5bn (-1.3%), while net revenue fell 1.4% to EUR 23.9bn. Net interest income paid the price normalisation and fell 4.3% to EUR 13.7bn, but held up well thanks to volume growth and a pass-through control on deposits (31%). Offsetting this are commissions and insurance management, up 5.6% to 8.7 billion, now accounting for some 35% of total revenues.

On the basis of these results, UniCredit is announcing total distributions of EUR 9.5 billion for the financial year 2025, an increase of 6% year-on-year. Of this, EUR 4.75 billion is earmarked for cash dividends, while the remainder is allocated to share buybacks, confirming a flexible approach to capital remuneration.
The dividend per share for FY25 rose to EUR 3.15, an increase of 31% year-on-year, reflecting both profit growth and a reduction in the number of outstanding shares.
